analysis.one_liner: Eases proof rules, pays miners' legal fees, and raises benefits for coal miners disabled by black lung disease.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action in the Senate and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Coal miners who develop black lung disease from years of breathing coal dust can file for federal disability benefits, but the claims process is slow, adversarial, and stacked against miners who often lack lawyers or good medical evidence. This bill would have shifted that balance: it would have let the Department of Labor pay miners' legal fees and medical-evaluation costs, made lung x-rays showing large opacities an automatic proof of total disability, resolved ties in the evidence in the miner's favor, reopened claims that were denied based on x-rays later found to be misread, raised the benefit amount with automatic inflation adjustments, and required a study of whether coal-dust limits should be lowered further. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners disabled by black lung disease and their surviving spouses and dependents. The bill would have guaranteed them legal help paid by the government, required coal companies to hand over all medical evidence in their files, given miners access to a CT scan and a government-funded pulmonary evaluation, presumed disability when x-rays show advanced disease, reopened denied claims that relied on discredited x-ray readings, raised monthly benefits starting in 2020, and indexed them to inflation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal miners with black lung disease

how_it_helps.text: Creates a program, paid from the Black Lung Disability Fund, to cover attorneys' fees (up to $4,500) and unreimbursed medical expenses (up to $3,000) for contested claims not decided within a year, with coal operators required to reimburse the fund when benefits are awarded [S3].

The bill's findings note that only 42 percent of claimants have an attorney at the initial determination and that some mine operators' lawyers have withheld medical evidence from claimants and judges; the bill requires all parties to disclose every piece of medical information, even if they do not plan to use it as evidence [S3].

Makes an x-ray showing a large opacity (over 1 centimeter) an irrebuttable presumption of total disability from black lung, restores the rule that evenly balanced evidence is resolved in the miner's favor, and lets claimants whose cases were decided on x-rays by discredited physician readers file new claims within one year [S3].

Raises the total-disability benefit to a fixed $8,370 per year starting in 2020 and indexes it to the Consumer Price Index, replacing the current tie to federal GS-2 pay, which pay freezes had frozen [S3].

Requires the Labor Department to develop a strategy to cut claim backlogs (claims took nearly a year to process, plus an average of 640 more days on appeal), authorizes CT scans in diagnosing complicated pneumoconiosis, and requires periodic studies of dust-monitor data to decide whether respirable coal dust limits should be lowered [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators, who would pay benefits and reimburse the fund for fees and medical-evaluation costs in winning claims, and the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund — financed by a coal excise tax — for costs where no liable operator can pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal mine operators and the black lung trust fund

drawbacks.text: The new fees, medical evaluations, and reopened claims are paid first from the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, which is financed by a coal excise tax; when operators are insolvent or liable operators cannot be charged, those costs fall on the industry-wide fund rather than the company responsible [S3].

The stricter evidence rules cut both ways in theory — the bill's new false-statement and disclosure provisions apply penalties to claimants and their attorneys as well as to operators, physicians, and insurers, with fines and up to five years' imprisonment for knowing misrepresentation [S3].

Automatic inflation indexing and a fixed 2020 benefit floor permanently raise federal outlays per claim, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge even while arguing it only restores what pay freezes took away [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go to a specific, severely harmed group — miners whose lungs were damaged on the job — and the costs are aimed mostly at the coal operators whose mines caused the exposure, with the shared trust fund as backstop. The main trade-off is money: permanent, inflation-indexed benefit increases and fee payments raise federal-program and industry costs, and reopened claims add workload to an adjudication system the bill itself acknowledges is badly backlogged. On balance the design targets the documented problems — withheld evidence, biased x-ray readings, and multi-year delays — rather than simply expanding eligibility broadly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bob Casey introduced the bill on July 23, 2019, joined by Senators Brown, Kaine, Warner, and Manchin [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day; that was the only action ever taken on it [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators are better off: they avoided new benefit liability, fee reimbursements, disclosure requirements, and possible stricter dust limits. Miners with black lung gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal operators; sick miners gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey Jr.
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Black Lung Benefits Improvement Act of 2019 on July 23, 2019.

for.name: Sens. Sherrod Brown, Tim Kaine, Mark Warner, and Joe Manchin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other senators signed on.

for.name: United Mine Workers of America
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed stronger black lung benefits and enforcement in this era, part of the broader coalition behind black lung reform legislation.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee (Chair Lamar Alexander)
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred on July 23, 2019; no hearing, markup, or vote occurred before the Congress ended.

against.name: Coal mine operators and their insurers
against.role: Coal industry employers who contest black lung claims
against.what_they_did: Historically contest black lung claims and oppose expansions of operator liability and stricter dust standards; no Senate committee action gave the bill no path forward.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-chaired committee never acted; no roll-call votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape rests on sponsorship and inaction rather than votes.

industries.note: Operators would pay benefits, reimburse the fund for claimants' legal fees and medical-evaluation costs, and face mandatory disclosure of all medical evidence plus possible sanctions and attorney disqualification for withholding or misrepresenting it. Stricter dust limits could also follow the required studies.

industries.industry: Black Lung Disability Trust Fund (financed by the coal excise tax)
industries.note: The fund would front attorneys' fees and medical-evaluation costs and absorb costs where operators cannot pay, but winning operators must reimburse it with interest. The coal excise tax that feeds the fund spreads those costs across the industry.
A new payment program would guarantee paid legal representation in contested claims, addressing the finding that only 42 percent of claimants have a lawyer at the initial determination.

industries.industry: Black lung clinics and NIOSH-certified B readers
industries.note: Clinics gain federal funding to help miners file claims, and physicians passing conflict-of-interest screening would perform government-paid evaluations. B readers with ties to coal companies or their law firms would be excluded from the qualified-physician list.
